title: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a positive integer k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k. Solve it with the prefix-sum remainder pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Subarray Sums Divisible by K (Prefix Remainder Counting)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum is a multiple of k. It is solved in linear time by tracking the running prefix sum's remainder modulo k and counting pairs of indices that share the same remainder, because two prefix sums with equal remainders bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k. Negative sums are normalized into a non-negative remainder before counting.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches summed to an exact multiple of a settlement unit k, say a multiple of five, because only multiples of the unit can be batched cleanly. As he walks he keeps a running total and looks only at its remainder when divided by k. Any two points in his walk that share the same remainder sandwich a stretch whose total is a clean multiple.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two prefix sums with the same remainder modulo k bound a subarray divisible by k, so count equal-remainder pairs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum is a multiple of k. It is solved in linear time by tracking the running prefix sum's remainder modulo k and counting pairs of indices that share the same remainder, because two prefix sums with equal remainders bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k. Negative sums are normalized into a non-negative remainder before counting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches summed to an exact multiple of a settlement unit k, say a multiple of five, because only multiples of the unit can be batched cleanly. As he walks he keeps a running total and looks only at its remainder when divided by k. Any two points in his walk that share the same remainder sandwich a stretch whose total is a clean multiple.

**One line to remember:** Two prefix sums with the same remainder modulo k bound a subarray divisible by k, so count equal-remainder pairs.

sections.s2_technical:
The key fact from modular arithmetic is that a subarray from index j plus one to index i has a sum divisible by k exactly when the prefix sum at i and the prefix sum at j leave the same remainder when divided by k. This is because the subarray sum is the difference of the two prefixes, and a difference is divisible by k precisely when the two values are congruent modulo k. So the problem reduces to counting, across all prefix sums, how many pairs share a remainder.

We maintain a running prefix sum and, at each step, compute its remainder modulo k. We keep a frequency array or map from remainder value to how many prefixes have produced that remainder so far. For each new prefix, the number of earlier prefixes with the same remainder is exactly the number of subarrays ending here that are divisible by k, so we add that count to our answer, then increment the frequency for the current remainder. We seed the remainder zero with a count of one before scanning, representing the empty prefix, so that a subarray from the start that is itself divisible by k is counted.

The subtlety that catches many candidates is negative numbers. In Java the percent operator can return a negative remainder, for example minus two modulo five is minus two rather than three. Since remainders must be compared consistently, we normalize with `int r = ((prefix % k) + k) % k;` so the remainder is always in the range zero to k minus one. Without this normalization, congruent prefixes of opposite sign would be bucketed separately and the count would be wrong. The senior-level nuance is exactly this remainder normalization, which is the signature correctness detail of the divisibility variant.

Because k is bounded we can use an `int[k]` frequency array instead of a map for speed. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass with constant-time remainder work, and the space complexity is O(k) for the remainder buckets. This prefix-remainder counting is the standard pattern for all divisible-sum subarray problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the batch-settlement team processes daily net flows and can only group a continuous stretch of days into a single settlement batch if the stretch's net total is an exact multiple of a settlement unit k, because the clearing house accepts only whole units. The team wants to count how many continuous stretches qualify, as a planning metric for how many clean batches the day's flows could form. Flows may be negative. This is exactly the subarrays-divisible-by-k counting problem.

Problem 2 — Testing divisibility for every possible stretch is quadratic and too slow at the bank's flow volume. The prefix-remainder counting method counts all divisible stretches in a single linear pass, correctly handling negative flows through remainder normalization, which makes the batch-planning metric fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `BatchDivisibilityCounter` service with a `countDivisibleStretches` method implementing prefix-remainder counting with normalization, and a runnable `SubarraysDivisibleByKDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's flow sequences against a unit k, logging each match at fine level and the final count at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's flows are 4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1 with unit k equal to 5. We seed the remainder-count array with remainder 0 having count 1, start the prefix at 0, and the answer at 0.

Step 1 at index 0, value 4: prefix becomes 4, remainder 4. Count of remainder 4 so far is 0, add 0. Increment remainder 4 to count 1.

Step 2 at index 1, value 5: prefix becomes 9, remainder 4. Count of remainder 4 is 1, add 1, count becomes 1. This is the stretch from index 1 to 1, the single 5 which is divisible by 5. Increment remainder 4 to count 2.

Step 3 at index 2, value 0: prefix becomes 9, remainder 4. Count of remainder 4 is 2, add 2, count becomes 3. Increment remainder 4 to count 3.

Step 4 at index 3, value -2: prefix becomes 7, remainder 2. Count of remainder 2 is 0, add 0. Increment remainder 2 to count 1.

Step 5 at index 4, value -3: prefix becomes 4, remainder 4. Count of remainder 4 is 3, add 3, count becomes 6. Increment remainder 4 to count 4.

Step 6 at index 5, value 1: prefix becomes 5, remainder 0. Count of remainder 0 is 1 from the seed, add 1, count becomes 7. Increment remainder 0 to count 2.

The count of divisible stretches for Rajesh is 7, matching the classic expected answer.

```

2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Day 1: remainder 4 seen 1 time(s) before → 1 divisible stretch(es)
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Day 2: remainder 4 seen 2 time(s) before → 2 divisible stretch(es)
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Day 4: remainder 4 seen 3 time(s) before → 3 divisible stretch(es)
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Day 5: remainder 0 seen 1 time(s) before → 1 divisible stretch(es)
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Divisible stretches (unit 5) over [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1] = 7
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Rajesh Kumar divisible stretches = 7
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Divisible stretches (unit 5) over [5, 10, 15] = 6
2026-10-27 18:52:00 INFO    Priya Sharma divisible stretches = 6
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k, in an array that may contain negatives, and I solve it in linear time with prefix sums reduced modulo k. The modular insight is that a subarray's sum is divisible by k exactly when the two prefix sums that bound it leave the same remainder, because their difference is divisible by k precisely when they are congruent. So I scan once keeping a running prefix, compute its remainder, and for each new prefix I add to my answer the number of earlier prefixes that shared the same remainder, then record the current remainder.

The correctness detail I always highlight is remainder normalization. In Java the percent operator can produce a negative result for negative prefixes, so I normalize with the running prefix modulo k, plus k, modulo k again, giving a remainder always between zero and k minus one. Without that step, congruent prefixes of opposite sign would land in different buckets and the count would be wrong. I also seed the remainder-zero bucket with a count of one before scanning, representing the empty prefix, so a subarray from the start that is itself divisible by k is counted.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the batch-settlement team. We processed daily net flows and could only group a continuous stretch of days into a single settlement batch if its net total was an exact multiple of a settlement unit, because the clearing house accepted only whole units, and we counted how many stretches qualified as a planning metric. Flows could be negative, so the remainder normalization was essential, and the prefix-remainder counting gave all divisible stretches in a single linear pass, scaling across the day's flows.

The senior-level point I make is that this is the divisibility cousin of the subarray-sum-equals-k problem, where I bucket by remainder instead of by exact prefix value, and recognizing that shared prefix-sum skeleton lets me adapt one pattern to many questions. I also stress the negative-remainder normalization as the single detail that distinguishes a correct implementation, and I mention using a fixed integer array of size k rather than a hash map since k is bounded, which removes boxing and speeds up the hot loop. Naming the normalization pitfall and the array optimization is what shows an interviewer I have actually implemented this correctly.
